topics.name: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
topics.summary: Electrons can leave a metal surface when they gain at least the work function \( \phi \): by heating (thermionic emission), by a strong electric field (field emission), or by light (photoelectric emission). In a photoelectric experiment, light falls on an emitter and a collector gathers the photoelectrons. The key observations are: emission occurs only if the frequency \( f \) is at least the threshold frequency \( f_0 \), however intense the light; emission is practically instantaneous; the photocurrent, and its saturation value, is proportional to intensity; and the stopping potential \( V_0 \), the negative collector potential that just stops the fastest electrons, depends on frequency but not on intensity. Intensity therefore controls HOW MANY electrons are emitted, while frequency controls HOW ENERGETIC the fastest ones are. The wave theory of light cannot explain these facts, which led Einstein to the photon picture.
key_formulas: Emission only if \( f\ge f_0 \), equivalently \( \lambda_{light}\le\lambda_0 \)
topics.worked_example: The stopping potential is 2 V and the saturation current is \( 3.2\times10^{-6} \) A. Then \( KE_{max}=eV_0=2 \) eV, and electrons per second \( =\dfrac{3.2\times10^{-6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=2\times10^{13} \). If the intensity is doubled, the current doubles but \( V_0 \) stays 2 V.
common_mistakes: Thinking brighter light raises \( KE_{max} \) or \( V_0 \); intensity changes only the number of electrons.
Thinking very intense light below \( f_0 \) can eventually eject electrons; no emission occurs at all.
Thinking higher frequency at the same intensity raises the saturation current.
Expecting a time delay for dim light; emission is instantaneous.

topics.name: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
topics.summary: Einstein treated light as photons of energy \( hf \). One photon gives all its energy to one electron, which spends at least the work function \( \phi \) to escape; the least-bound electrons leave with \( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \). Since \( KE_{max}=eV_0 \), we get \( V_0=\dfrac{h}{e}f-\dfrac{\phi}{e} \). At threshold \( KE_{max}=0 \), so \( \phi=hf_0=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} \), where \( f_0 \) and \( \lambda_0 \) are the metal's threshold values, not the incident light's. The work function is a property of each metal (caesium about 1.9 eV, sodium about 2.3 eV, zinc about 3.7 eV), unlike the universal constants \( h \), \( c \) and \( e \). A graph of \( V_0 \) against \( f \) is a straight line whose slope \( h/e \) is the same for every metal, while its intercepts (\( f_0 \) on the frequency axis and \( -\phi/e \) on the \( V_0 \) axis) change from metal to metal.
topics.worked_example: Light of 414 nm falls on caesium (\( \phi=1.9 \) eV). Photon energy \( =\dfrac{1242}{414}=3 \) eV, so \( KE_{max}=3-1.9=1.1 \) eV and \( V_0=1.1 \) V. Caesium's threshold wavelength is \( \lambda_0=\dfrac{1242}{1.9} \) nm, longer than 414 nm, consistent with emission.
common_mistakes: Using the incident frequency or wavelength in \( \phi=hf_0=hc/\lambda_0 \) instead of the threshold values.
Treating \( \phi \) as a universal constant; it differs from metal to metal.
Saying the slope of the \( V_0 \)-\( f \) graph depends on the metal; it is always \( h/e \), and only the intercepts change.
Assuming \( KE_{max} \) is proportional to \( f \); the constant \( \phi \) makes it more than double when \( f \) doubles.

topics.name: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
topics.summary: A photon is a quantum of light with energy \( E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}} \) and momentum \( p=\dfrac{E}{c}=\dfrac{h}{\lambda_{light}} \). Photons have zero rest mass, are electrically neutral (so fields do not deflect them), and all travel at \( c \) in vacuum whatever their frequency. The energy of each photon depends only on frequency; the intensity of a beam depends on how many photons cross unit area per second. For a source of power \( P \), the number of photons emitted per second is \( \dfrac{P}{hf} \), so at the same power, lower-frequency (redder) light contains more photons. A fully absorbed beam delivers momentum at a rate equal to a force. Light therefore shows a dual nature: wave behaviour in interference and diffraction, and particle behaviour when it exchanges energy with matter, as in the photoelectric effect.
topics.worked_example: For 663 nm light with \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s: \( p=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.63\times10^{-7}}=1\times10^{-27} \) kg m/s and \( E=pc=3\times10^{-19} \) J \( =1.875 \) eV. A 3 mW beam emits \( \dfrac{3\times10^{-3}}{3\times10^{-19}}=1\times10^{16} \) photons per second.
common_mistakes: Thinking higher intensity means more energetic photons; it means more photons.
Confusing photon energy \( hc/\lambda_{light} \) with photon momentum \( h/\lambda_{light} \).
Forgetting to convert nm to m, or J to eV.
Thinking photons of different colours travel at different speeds in vacuum.

topics.name: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
topics.summary: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has an associated wavelength \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{mv} \). Writing \( p=\sqrt{2mKE} \), \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}} \), and for a charge \( q \) accelerated from rest through \( V \), \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} \). For an electron this becomes \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt V} \) nm. At the same momentum, all particles have the same wavelength; at the same kinetic energy, \( \lambda\propto1/\sqrt m \), so a lighter particle such as an electron has a longer wavelength than a proton or an alpha particle. The hypothesis applies to all matter, including cricket balls and dust grains; their wavelengths are simply far too small to observe because their masses are large. This wave nature of matter mirrors the particle nature of light and completes the dual picture.
topics.worked_example: An electron accelerated through 100 V has \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{100}}=0.1227 \) nm. A proton and an alpha particle through the same voltage have \( \dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha}=\sqrt{\dfrac{4\times2}{1\times1}}=2\sqrt2 \), so the lighter proton has the longer wavelength.
common_mistakes: Giving the heavier particle the larger wavelength at equal kinetic energy; \( \lambda\propto1/\sqrt m \).
Claiming de Broglie waves exist only for microscopic particles; they apply to all matter.
Forgetting the square root, e.g. taking \( \lambda\propto1/V \) instead of \( 1/\sqrt V \).
Ignoring charge when comparing particles accelerated through the same voltage.

topics.name: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
topics.summary: Davisson and Germer (1927) fired electrons from a heated filament, accelerated through a known voltage, at a nickel crystal and measured the intensity of scattered electrons at different angles. At 54 V a sharp intensity peak appeared at \( 50^{\circ} \), just like X-ray diffraction from a crystal. The regular atomic planes acted as a grating whose spacing (about 0.1 nm) matches the electron's de Broglie wavelength; the theoretical value 0.167 nm agreed well with the measured 0.165 nm, confirming de Broglie's hypothesis. Raising the voltage shortens the wavelength and moves the diffraction peak to smaller angles. Matter-wave diffraction has since been seen for neutrons, atoms and molecules; thermal neutrons are widely used for crystal studies. Heavier particles at the same voltage have much smaller wavelengths. The short wavelength of fast electrons is also why electron microscopes resolve far finer detail than optical ones.
topics.worked_example: Electrons accelerated through 400 V have \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{400}}=0.06135 \) nm. Raising 54 V to 216 V (four times) halves the wavelength from 0.167 nm to 0.0835 nm, so the diffraction peak moves to a smaller angle.
common_mistakes: Saying the experiment shows the particle nature of light; it shows the wave nature of electrons.
Thinking only electrons have matter waves; neutrons, atoms and molecules diffract too.
Expecting heavier particles at the same voltage to have longer wavelengths.
Concluding electrons are only waves; matter has a dual nature.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, what is the name given to the minimum frequency of incident light below which no photoelectrons are emitted from a given metal?
questions.explanation:
Every metal has a characteristic minimum frequency, the threshold frequency \( f_0 \).

If the incident frequency \( f \) is below \( f_0 \), no electrons are emitted at all, whatever the intensity.
questions.hint: The word describes a 'doorway' value that must be crossed before anything happens.
distractor_logic: Saturation refers to the photocurrent reaching a maximum, not to any frequency.
Stopping refers to the stopping potential \( V_0 \), a voltage, not a frequency.
Intensity has no cut-off role; emission is decided by frequency, not by how bright the light is.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Light of a fixed frequency above the threshold falls on a metal. If only the intensity of the light is increased, what happens?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons increases
The photocurrent increases because more photoelectrons are emitted per second
The photocurrent decreases because the electrons get less energy each
questions.explanation:
Intensity decides how many photons arrive per second, and hence how many electrons are emitted per second.

Each electron still gets the energy of one photon, so the maximum kinetic energy and the stopping potential do not change. Only the current increases.
questions.hint: Brighter light means more photons, not more energetic photons.
distractor_logic: Intensity does not change the energy of each photon, so maximum kinetic energy is unaffected.
Stopping potential depends on maximum kinetic energy, which intensity cannot change.
More photons means more electrons, so the current rises rather than falls.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Light whose frequency is below the threshold frequency \( f_0 \) of a metal is made extremely intense and falls on the metal. What is observed?
options: Electrons are emitted after a short time delay
Electrons are emitted but with very small kinetic energy
No photoelectric emission occurs at all
Electrons are emitted because the high intensity supplies enough energy
questions.explanation:
An electron absorbs energy from one photon at a time, and each photon has energy \( hf \).

If \( f
questions.hint: Think about the energy carried by ONE photon, not by the whole beam.
distractor_logic: Emission is instantaneous when it happens at all; energy does not build up over time below threshold.
Below threshold there are no electrons emitted, not slow ones.
This is the wave-theory prediction that the photoelectric effect disproves; intensity cannot replace frequency.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when the metal is heated to a high temperature is called:
questions.explanation:
Heating gives the free electrons enough thermal energy to overcome the work function \( \phi \) of the metal.

This method is called thermionic emission, used for example in the filament of an electron gun.
questions.hint: The prefix of the correct term is related to heat.
distractor_logic: Photoelectric emission uses light, not heat, to free electrons.
Field emission uses a very strong electric field, not heating.
Secondary emission is caused by bombarding the surface with fast particles, not by heating.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: How much time passes between the incidence of suitable light (frequency above threshold) on a metal and the emission of photoelectrons?
options: Practically none; emission is instantaneous (of the order of \( 10^{-9} \) s or less)
A few seconds, and longer for dim light
A time that increases as the frequency increases
A time that depends only on the stopping potential
questions.explanation:
Experiments show emission starts almost instantly, even for very dim light.

This is because a single photon gives its whole energy to a single electron in one event; no energy has to accumulate.
questions.hint: Remember what the photon picture says about how energy is delivered.
distractor_logic: Dim light only reduces the number of electrons, not how quickly the first one appears.
Higher frequency gives more energetic electrons, not a longer delay.
Stopping potential measures kinetic energy; it has nothing to do with a time delay.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: In a photoelectric experiment, the collector is made negative with respect to the emitter. The minimum magnitude of this negative potential at which the photocurrent becomes zero is called the:
questions.explanation:
A negative collector potential repels photoelectrons.

When it is just enough to stop even the most energetic electrons, the current becomes zero. This value is the stopping potential \( V_0 \).
questions.hint: This potential 'stops' the fastest electrons.
distractor_logic: An accelerating potential is positive and increases the current rather than stopping it.
Saturation is when the current becomes maximum, the opposite situation.
Work function \( \phi \) is an energy of the metal, not an applied potential.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: As the positive potential of the collector is increased, the photocurrent rises and then becomes constant. This constant value is called the:
questions.explanation:
Once the collector potential is high enough, every emitted electron reaches the collector.

Increasing the potential further cannot increase the current, so it saturates. The saturation current depends on the intensity of the light.
questions.hint: The current cannot grow once ALL emitted electrons are already collected.
distractor_logic: There is no 'stopping current'; at the stopping potential the current is zero.
Threshold is a term used for frequency or wavelength, not for the current.
Leakage current is not the maximum photocurrent reached at high positive potential.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: For a given metal, the stopping potential \( V_0 \) depends on:
options: The intensity of the incident light only
Both the intensity and the frequency of the incident light
Neither; it is a fixed constant for the metal
The frequency of the incident light only
questions.explanation:
\( eV_0 \) equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

Maximum kinetic energy depends on the energy of each photon, \( hf \), so \( V_0 \) depends on frequency. Intensity only changes the number of electrons.
questions.hint: Stopping potential measures the energy of the FASTEST electron.
distractor_logic: Intensity controls only the number of electrons, not their energy.
Adding intensity to the list is the common trap; intensity has no effect on \( V_0 \).
\( V_0 \) changes when the frequency changes, so it is not fixed for a metal.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Which of the following is Einstein's photoelectric equation?
questions.explanation:
A photon gives energy \( hf \) to one electron.

The electron uses \( \phi \) to escape, and the rest appears as kinetic energy: \( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \).
questions.hint: Energy in minus energy spent on escaping equals energy left over.
distractor_logic: Adding \( \phi \) would mean escaping gives the electron energy instead of costing it.
This would make \( KE_{max} \) negative whenever emission actually occurs.
Energy balance is a subtraction, not a ratio.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: The work function \( \phi \) of a metal is related to its threshold frequency \( f_0 \) by:
options: \( \phi=hf \), where \( f \) is the incident frequency
questions.explanation:
At threshold, the photon has just enough energy to free an electron with zero kinetic energy.

So \( hf_0-\phi=0 \), giving \( \phi=hf_0 \).
questions.hint: At threshold, the kinetic energy of the emitted electron is zero.
distractor_logic: The incident frequency describes the light, not the metal; \( \phi \) uses the threshold value.
Dividing by \( h \) does not give an energy.
\( h/f_0 \) has units of J s squared, not energy.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Photons of energy 5 eV fall on a metal of work function \( \phi=2 \) eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
questions.explanation:
\( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \).

\( KE_{max}=5-2=3 \) eV.
questions.hint: Subtract the escape energy from the photon energy.
distractor_logic: The work function was added instead of subtracted.
The ratio \( 5/2 \) is not an energy balance.
Multiplying the energies has no physical meaning here.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Sodium has work function \( \phi=2.3 \) eV. Light whose photons each carry 2 eV falls on it. What happens?
options: Electrons are emitted with maximum kinetic energy 0.3 eV
Electrons are emitted with maximum kinetic energy 4.3 eV
Electrons are emitted and the stopping potential is 0.3 V
No photoelectric emission occurs, since each photon has less energy than \( \phi \)
questions.explanation:
Emission needs \( hf\ge\phi \).

Here \( 2 \) eV \( <2.3 \) eV, so no electron can escape. No emission occurs at all; there is no kinetic energy or stopping potential to calculate.
questions.hint: Compare photon energy with the work function before subtracting.
distractor_logic: Subtracting the wrong way round gives a meaningless positive number.
Adding the energies ignores that escaping costs energy.
A stopping potential needs emitted electrons, and there are none.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Which statement about the work function \( \phi \) is correct?
options: It is a property of the metal surface and differs from one metal to another
It is a universal constant, the same for every metal, like \( h \)
It depends on the frequency of the incident light
It depends on the intensity of the incident light
questions.explanation:
\( \phi \) is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a particular metal.

It depends on the metal (e.g. caesium about 1.9 eV, zinc about 3.7 eV), not on the light used.
questions.hint: Different metals have different threshold frequencies.
distractor_logic: Unlike \( h \), \( c \) and \( e \), the work function changes from metal to metal.
The light is what is supplied; \( \phi \) is what the metal demands.
Intensity affects only the number of electrons, not the metal's binding.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: The threshold wavelength \( \lambda_0 \) of a metal with work function \( \phi \) is:
questions.explanation:
At threshold, \( \phi=hf_0=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} \).

Rearranging gives \( \lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{\phi} \).
questions.hint: Start from \( \phi=hc/\lambda_0 \).
distractor_logic: This is the reciprocal of the correct expression.
Multiplying gives units of energy squared times length, not a wavelength.
Missing \( c \); \( h/\phi \) has units of time, not length.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Metal X has a smaller work function than metal Y. Compared with Y, metal X has:
options: A higher threshold frequency and a longer threshold wavelength
A lower threshold frequency and a shorter threshold wavelength
A lower threshold frequency and a longer threshold wavelength
The same threshold frequency, since \( f_0 \) is universal
questions.explanation:
\( f_0=\dfrac{\phi}{h} \), so a smaller \( \phi \) means a smaller \( f_0 \).

\( \lambda_0=\dfrac{c}{f_0} \), so a smaller \( f_0 \) means a longer \( \lambda_0 \).
questions.hint: Frequency and wavelength move in opposite directions.
distractor_logic: \( f_0 \) is proportional to \( \phi \), so it cannot be higher.
A lower frequency always pairs with a longer wavelength.
\( f_0 \) depends on \( \phi \), which differs between metals.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: In terms of the stopping potential \( V_0 \), Einstein's photoelectric equation is written as:
questions.explanation:
The stopping potential satisfies \( eV_0=KE_{max} \).

Combining with \( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \) gives \( eV_0=hf-\phi \).
questions.hint: Replace \( KE_{max} \) by \( eV_0 \).
distractor_logic: The work function must be subtracted, not added.
\( hf_0 \) is simply \( \phi \); the incident frequency is missing.
This has the wrong sign and would be negative whenever emission occurs.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: The energy \( E \) of a photon of light with frequency \( f \) and wavelength \( \lambda_{light} \) is:
questions.explanation:
Planck-Einstein relation: \( E=hf \).

Since \( f=c/\lambda_{light} \), \( E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}} \).
questions.hint: Energy grows with frequency.
distractor_logic: Dividing by \( f \) would make higher-frequency photons less energetic.
Multiplying by wavelength makes longer waves more energetic, which is backwards.
\( hf/c \) is the photon's momentum, not its energy.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: The momentum \( p \) of a photon of energy \( E \) and wavelength \( \lambda_{light} \) is:
questions.explanation:
A photon's momentum is \( p=\dfrac{E}{c} \).

Using \( E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}} \): \( p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda_{light}} \).
questions.hint: Divide the photon energy by the speed of light.
distractor_logic: Multiplying by wavelength or by \( c \) gives the wrong units and trend.
\( hc/\lambda_{light} \) is the photon energy, not momentum.
\( E/c^{2} \) has units of mass, not momentum.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: What is the rest mass of a photon?
options: Equal to the mass of an electron
It increases with the frequency of the light
questions.explanation:
A photon always travels at \( c \) and can never be at rest.

Its rest mass is zero, even though it carries energy \( hf \) and momentum \( h/\lambda_{light} \).
questions.hint: Can a photon ever be brought to rest?
distractor_logic: Photons and electrons are completely different particles.
\( h/c^{2} \) is not even a mass in general; it lacks a frequency factor.
Energy and momentum grow with frequency, but rest mass stays zero.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: In vacuum, photons of red light and photons of violet light travel with:
options: Speeds that depend on the intensity of the beam
questions.explanation:
All photons move at \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s in vacuum.

Their frequencies differ, so their energies and momenta differ, but not their speed.
questions.hint: The speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant.
distractor_logic: Frequency changes energy, not speed in vacuum.
Wavelength changes momentum, not speed in vacuum.
Intensity only changes the number of photons, not their speed.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A beam of monochromatic light is made more intense without changing its frequency. In the photon picture, this means:
options: More photons cross unit area per second, each with the same energy as before
The same number of photons, each with more energy
More photons, each with more energy
Fewer photons, each with more energy
questions.explanation:
Photon energy is \( hf \), fixed by frequency.

Intensity is energy per unit area per second, so higher intensity at the same \( f \) means more photons per unit area per second.
questions.hint: Which quantity sets each photon's energy?
distractor_logic: Photon energy depends only on frequency, which is unchanged.
The number increases, but each photon's energy stays \( hf \).
Neither half is right: the number rises and the energy is unchanged.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A beam of photons passes through a region containing a magnetic field. What happens to the photons?
options: They bend in a circle like electrons
They pass undeflected, because photons are electrically neutral
They are deflected opposite to electrons, like positive charges
They are stopped completely by the field
questions.explanation:
Magnetic and electric fields exert forces only on charged particles.

Photons carry no charge, so they are not deflected.
questions.hint: What property does a particle need to feel a magnetic force?
distractor_logic: Photons carry no charge, unlike electrons.
There is no positive charge on a photon either.
A static field does not absorb or stop neutral photons.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: If the wavelength of light is halved, the energy of each photon:
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}} \), so \( E\propto\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{light}} \).

Halving \( \lambda_{light} \) doubles \( E \).
questions.hint: Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
distractor_logic: This treats energy as directly proportional to wavelength.
Photon energy depends on wavelength, so it must change.
There is no square in \( E=hc/\lambda_{light} \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength \( \lambda_{light}=663 \) nm? (Take \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s.)
questions.explanation:
\( p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda_{light}} \) with \( \lambda_{light}=663\times10^{-9} \) m.

\( p=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.63\times10^{-7}}=1\times10^{-27} \) kg m/s.
questions.hint: Convert nm to m before dividing.
distractor_logic: The wavelength was used as 663 m instead of \( 663\times10^{-9} \) m.
This is the photon's energy in joules, not its momentum.
The ratio was inverted, giving \( \lambda_{light}/h \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength \( \lambda \) of a particle of momentum \( p \) is:
questions.explanation:
De Broglie proposed that a particle of momentum \( p \) has an associated wavelength \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p} \).

The same relation holds for photons, which is what inspired it.
questions.hint: Larger momentum should mean a shorter wavelength.
distractor_logic: This is the reciprocal; it would give wavelength growing with momentum.
A product also makes wavelength grow with momentum.
There is no square of momentum in the de Broglie relation.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: Who first proposed that moving material particles have wave properties?
questions.explanation:
In 1924 de Broglie suggested that matter, like radiation, has a dual nature, with \( \lambda=h/p \).

Davisson and Germer later confirmed it experimentally.
questions.hint: The wavelength formula is named after him.
distractor_logic: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect using photons of light.
Davisson and Germer verified the idea by experiment; they did not propose it.
Planck introduced energy quanta for radiation, not matter waves.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: Does a moving cricket ball have a de Broglie wavelength?
options: No, de Broglie waves exist only for microscopic particles such as electrons
No, because a cricket ball carries no electric charge
Yes, but its wavelength is far too small to detect because of its large mass
Yes, and its wavelength is large enough to observe diffraction through a doorway
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv} \) applies to every moving object.

For a ball, \( mv \) is huge compared with \( h \), so \( \lambda \) is immeasurably tiny. The formula still applies; the effect is just undetectable.
questions.hint: Put a large mass into \( \lambda=h/(mv) \).
distractor_logic: The hypothesis covers all matter; smallness of \( \lambda \) is the only reason it is unseen.
Charge plays no part in \( \lambda=h/p \); neutrons have matter waves too.
The wavelength is many orders of magnitude smaller than any doorway.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: If the momentum of a particle is doubled, its de Broglie wavelength becomes:
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p} \), so \( \lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{p} \).

Doubling \( p \) halves \( \lambda \).
questions.hint: Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.
distractor_logic: This treats \( \lambda \) as proportional to \( p \).
This treats \( \lambda \) as proportional to \( p^{2} \).
This wrongly uses an inverse-square dependence.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \( m \) and kinetic energy \( KE \) is:
questions.explanation:
\( KE=\dfrac{p^{2}}{2m} \), so \( p=\sqrt{2mKE} \).

Hence \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}} \).
questions.hint: Express momentum in terms of kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: The square root was dropped; \( 2mKE \) is \( p^{2} \), not \( p \).
This is the reciprocal of the correct expression.
Multiplying makes \( \lambda \) grow with energy, which is backwards.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: An electron and a proton have the same momentum. How do their de Broglie wavelengths compare?
options: They differ because the charges have opposite signs
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p} \) depends only on momentum.

Equal momenta give equal wavelengths, regardless of mass or charge.
questions.hint: Which quantity alone appears in \( \lambda=h/p \)?
distractor_logic: The electron's lower mass matters only when KE or speed, not momentum, is the same.
With equal momentum, the proton's larger mass has no effect on \( \lambda \).
Charge does not appear in \( \lambda=h/p \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: A particle of mass \( m \) and charge \( q \) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference \( V \). Its de Broglie wavelength is:
questions.explanation:
The particle gains \( KE=qV \).

\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} \).
questions.hint: The kinetic energy gained is \( qV \).
distractor_logic: The square root is missing.
The factor 2 from \( KE=p^{2}/2m \) is missing.
This expression has no physical derivation and wrong dimensions.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: A ball of mass 0.1 kg moves at 6.63 m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (Take \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s.)
questions.explanation:
\( p=mv=0.1\times6.63=0.663 \) kg m/s.

\( \lambda=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{0.663}=1\times10^{-33} \) m, far too small to observe.
questions.hint: Find \( p=mv \) first.
distractor_logic: The speed was left out, dividing \( h \) by the mass only.
The ratio was inverted.
The mass was taken as 100 (grams) instead of 0.1 kg.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: The Davisson-Germer experiment provided experimental confirmation of:
questions.explanation:
Davisson and Germer observed electrons being diffracted by a crystal.

Diffraction is a wave property, so this confirmed de Broglie's matter waves for electrons.
questions.hint: The experiment showed electrons doing something only waves do.
distractor_logic: The particle nature of light is shown by the photoelectric effect.
Photons are shown by the photoelectric effect, not by electron diffraction.
Charge quantisation was established by Millikan's oil-drop experiment.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: What was used as the target in the Davisson-Germer experiment?
questions.explanation:
A beam of electrons was directed at a nickel crystal.

The regular rows of nickel atoms acted as a diffraction grating for the electron waves.
questions.hint: The target had to be a regular crystal lattice of a metal.
distractor_logic: Gold foil was used in Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment.
A zinc plate is associated with photoelectric experiments.
Sodium is a common photoelectric emitter, not the diffraction target here.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Which phenomenon did Davisson and Germer observe with the electron beam?
options: Diffraction of electrons by the crystal
Deflection of electrons by a magnetic field
questions.explanation:
The scattered electron intensity showed a sharp peak at a particular angle.

This is a diffraction maximum, exactly like X-rays from a crystal.
questions.hint: The result looked like X-ray crystal diffraction.
distractor_logic: No light was used to eject electrons in this experiment.
The beam was of electrons, not light.
Magnetic deflection shows charge, not wave nature.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Why was a crystal needed to show electron diffraction, rather than an ordinary slit?
options: Crystals are the only materials that electrons cannot pass through
Crystals emit electrons when struck by light
Electrons diffract only through magnetic materials
The spacing between atoms in a crystal is comparable to the electron's de Broglie wavelength (about 0.1 nm)
questions.explanation:
Diffraction is noticeable only when the grating spacing is comparable to the wavelength.

Electron wavelengths are about 0.1 nm, matching interatomic spacing in crystals; ordinary slits are far too wide.
questions.hint: Diffraction needs spacing comparable to wavelength.
distractor_logic: The crystal scattered the electrons; impenetrability is not the reason.
Photoemission plays no role in producing the diffraction.
Magnetism is irrelevant; the atomic spacing is what matters.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, the strongest diffraction peak was observed for electrons accelerated through:
questions.explanation:
The sharp peak appeared at an accelerating voltage of 54 V and a scattering angle of \( 50^{\circ} \).

The corresponding de Broglie wavelength is about 0.167 nm.
questions.hint: It is a small voltage of a few tens of volts.
distractor_logic: 54 kV would give a far shorter wavelength than was observed.
The decimal point is misplaced.
100 V is a common textbook example, not the observed peak value.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: The Davisson-Germer experiment is closely analogous to:
options: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.explanation:
In both, waves with wavelength near 0.1 nm are diffracted by the regular atomic planes of a crystal.

The electron pattern resembled the X-ray pattern, showing electrons behave as waves.
questions.hint: Which other experiment uses a crystal as a diffraction grating?
distractor_logic: Rutherford scattering reveals the nucleus, not wave behaviour.
The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of light.
Refraction by a prism does not involve atomic-scale gratings.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer apparatus, the electron beam is produced by:
options: Photoelectric emission from a zinc plate
Radioactive decay of the nickel target
Thermionic emission from a heated filament
Field emission from the nickel crystal
questions.explanation:
An electron gun heats a tungsten filament coated with barium oxide so that it emits electrons.

These are then accelerated through a chosen voltage towards the crystal.
questions.hint: The source is an electron gun with a filament.
distractor_logic: No light source is used to produce the beam.
The nickel target scatters electrons; it is not a radioactive source.
The crystal is the target, not the emitter.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Matter-wave diffraction has been observed not only for electrons but also for:
options: No other particles; it is unique to electrons
Only other charged particles, such as protons
Neutrons, and even atoms and molecules
questions.explanation:
De Broglie's relation applies to all matter.

Neutron diffraction is routinely used to study crystals, and diffraction of atoms and molecules has also been demonstrated.
questions.hint: Matter waves are not limited by charge.
distractor_logic: Wave behaviour belongs to all matter, not just electrons.
Neutral neutrons diffract, so charge is not needed.
Massive particles have matter waves; this is the whole point of de Broglie's idea.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Photocurrent versus collector potential graphs are drawn for light of the same frequency but two intensities, \( I_1>I_2 \). How do the two curves compare?
options: Same stopping potential; the curve for \( I_1 \) has the larger saturation current
Different stopping potentials; the same saturation current
Different stopping potentials and different saturation currents
The curve for \( I_1 \) has both a larger stopping potential and a larger saturation current
questions.explanation:
Same frequency means the same maximum kinetic energy, so both curves cut the potential axis at the same \( -V_0 \).

Higher intensity gives more electrons per second, so the saturation current is higher for \( I_1 \).
questions.hint: Which quantity depends on frequency and which on intensity?
distractor_logic: This swaps the roles: intensity changes current, not stopping potential.
Stopping potential cannot differ when the frequency is the same.
Higher intensity does not give a larger stopping potential; that is the central intensity trap.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Photocurrent versus collector potential graphs are drawn for two frequencies \( f_1>f_2 \) (both above threshold) at the same intensity. Which statement is correct?
options: The saturation current is larger for \( f_1 \), and the stopping potentials are equal
The saturation currents are equal, but the stopping potential is larger in magnitude for \( f_1 \)
Both the saturation current and the stopping potential are larger for \( f_1 \)
The stopping potential is larger in magnitude for \( f_2 \)
questions.explanation:
At the same intensity, the saturation current is the same.

Higher frequency means more energetic photons, so the maximum kinetic energy and hence \( V_0 \) are larger for \( f_1 \).
questions.hint: Frequency decides the energy of each electron.
distractor_logic: Raising frequency at fixed intensity does not raise the photocurrent; that is a trap.
Only the stopping potential changes with frequency here, not the saturation current.
Lower frequency gives lower maximum kinetic energy, so \( f_2 \) has the smaller \( V_0 \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The intensity of light (frequency above threshold) falling on a metal is doubled. Which pair of changes is correct?
options: Number of photoelectrons per second is unchanged; maximum kinetic energy doubles
Both the number per second and the maximum kinetic energy double
Number of photoelectrons per second doubles; maximum kinetic energy is unchanged
Number per second doubles; maximum kinetic energy halves
questions.explanation:
Doubling intensity at fixed frequency doubles the number of photons per second, so twice as many electrons are emitted.

The energy of each photon, \( hf \), is unchanged, so the maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.
questions.hint: Each electron still interacts with just one photon.
distractor_logic: This swaps intensity and frequency effects completely.
Intensity cannot raise maximum kinetic energy, so it cannot double.
There is no mechanism for more photons to lower the energy each electron receives.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment is measured as 2 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
The work done by the stopping potential on the fastest electron equals its kinetic energy: \( KE_{max}=eV_0 \).

\( KE_{max}=e\times2 \) V \( =2 \) eV \( =2\times1.6\times10^{-19} \) J \( =3.2\times10^{-19} \) J.
questions.hint: An electron crossing 1 V gains or loses 1 eV.
distractor_logic: Halving the potential has no basis; \( KE_{max}=eV_0 \) directly.
Doubling comes from wrongly using \( \tfrac12 \) or \( 2 \) factors from kinetic energy formulas.
The charge \( e \) was forgotten; 2 V times 1 C would give 2 J, which is absurd for one electron.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Why does the wave theory of light fail to explain the existence of a threshold frequency?
options: Wave theory says energy absorbed depends on intensity, so any frequency should eject electrons if the light is intense enough
Wave theory says light cannot carry energy at all
Wave theory predicts that only high-frequency light can be absorbed
Wave theory predicts that electrons are emitted only below a certain frequency
questions.explanation:
In the wave picture, energy is spread continuously over the wavefront and grows with intensity.

So a strong enough beam of any frequency should eventually free electrons. Experiments show no emission below \( f_0 \), which the wave theory cannot explain.
questions.hint: In the wave picture, what decides the energy delivered to the surface?
distractor_logic: Wave theory certainly treats light as carrying energy; its issue is how that energy depends on intensity.
If wave theory predicted a frequency cut-off, it would not fail here.
This reverses the observation and is not a wave-theory prediction.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Monochromatic light falls on a metal, yet the photoelectrons emerge with kinetic energies ranging from zero up to a maximum value. Why?
options: Monochromatic light contains photons of many different energies
Electrons come from different depths and energy states, so they lose different amounts of energy before escaping
The intensity of the light varies from point to point
Each electron absorbs a different number of photons
questions.explanation:
Every photon has the same energy \( hf \).

Electrons deeper in the metal or more tightly bound use up more energy in escaping, so they come out slower. Only the least bound surface electrons leave with \( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \).
questions.hint: All photons are identical; look at the electrons instead.
distractor_logic: Monochromatic means a single frequency, so all photons have the same energy.
Intensity variations change numbers of electrons, not their individual energies.
In the photoelectric effect one electron absorbs exactly one photon.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The saturation photocurrent in a photoelectric experiment (frequency fixed above threshold) is directly proportional to:
options: The frequency of the incident light
The intensity of the incident light
The square of the frequency of the incident light
questions.explanation:
Saturation current is reached when all emitted electrons are collected.

The number emitted per second is proportional to the number of photons per second, which is proportional to intensity.
questions.hint: Current counts electrons per second.
distractor_logic: Frequency affects the energy of electrons, not how many are emitted.
Stopping potential relates to energy, and saturation current relates to number; they are independent.
There is no square-of-frequency dependence for the current.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The frequency of light falling on a photosensitive metal is increased (staying above threshold). What happens to the stopping potential?
questions.explanation:
A higher frequency means each photon has more energy, \( hf \).

So the maximum kinetic energy increases, and a larger retarding potential \( V_0 \) is needed to stop the fastest electrons.
questions.hint: More energetic photons produce more energetic electrons.
distractor_logic: Stopping potential moves in the same direction as frequency, not opposite.
Being unchanged is the behaviour under an intensity change, not a frequency change.
Stopping potential is zero only at exactly the threshold frequency.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Light of wavelength \( \lambda_{light}=414 \) nm falls on caesium (\( \phi=1.9 \) eV). What is the stopping potential? (Take \( h=4.14\times10^{-15} \) eV s and \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, so \( hc=1242 \) eV nm.)
questions.explanation:
Photon energy: \( hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}}=\dfrac{1242}{414}=3 \) eV.

\( KE_{max}=3-1.9=1.1 \) eV, so \( V_0=1.1 \) V.
questions.hint: Find the photon energy in eV first.
distractor_logic: This is the photon energy, with the work function not subtracted.
The work function was added to the photon energy.
This is just the work function written as a voltage.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: A metal has work function \( \phi=2.07 \) eV. What is its threshold wavelength \( \lambda_0 \)? (Take \( h=4.14\times10^{-15} \) eV s and \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, so \( hc=1242 \) eV nm.)
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{\phi} \).

\( \lambda_0=\dfrac{1242}{2.07}=600 \) nm.
questions.hint: Divide \( hc \) by the work function.
distractor_logic: Using \( 2\phi \) in the denominator halves the answer.
Using \( \phi/2 \) in the denominator doubles the answer.
414 nm corresponds to 3 eV, not 2.07 eV.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Light of frequency \( 8\times10^{14} \) Hz falls on a metal whose threshold frequency is \( f_0=5\times10^{14} \) Hz. What is the work function of the metal? (Take \( h=4.14\times10^{-15} \) eV s.)
questions.explanation:
The work function uses the threshold frequency, not the incident one: \( \phi=hf_0 \).

\( \phi=4.14\times10^{-15}\times5\times10^{14}=2.07 \) eV.
questions.hint: Which frequency belongs to the metal itself?
distractor_logic: This uses the incident frequency \( 8\times10^{14} \) Hz instead of \( f_0 \).
This is \( h(f-f_0) \), which is \( KE_{max} \), not \( \phi \).
This adds \( hf \) and \( hf_0 \), mixing the incident and threshold values.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Light of wavelength \( \lambda_{light}=310.5 \) nm produces photoelectrons with stopping potential 2 V from a metal. What is the work function? (Take \( h=4.14\times10^{-15} \) eV s and \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, so \( hc=1242 \) eV nm.)
questions.explanation:
Photon energy: \( \dfrac{1242}{310.5}=4 \) eV.

\( \phi=hf-eV_0=4-2=2 \) eV.
questions.hint: Work function = photon energy minus maximum kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: The kinetic energy was added to the photon energy.
This is the photon energy itself, taking \( KE_{max} \) as zero.
The difference was halved without reason.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: A graph of maximum kinetic energy \( KE_{max} \) of photoelectrons against incident frequency \( f \) is a straight line. Its slope equals:
questions.explanation:
\( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \) has the form \( y=mx+c \) with \( m=h \).

The slope is \( h \), the same for all metals. (The slope \( h/e \) belongs to the \( V_0 \)-versus-\( f \) graph.)
questions.hint: Match \( KE_{max}=hf-\phi \) with the straight-line form.
distractor_logic: \( h/e \) is the slope when \( V_0 \), not \( KE_{max} \), is plotted.
\( \phi \) appears in the intercept, not the slope.
This is the reciprocal of the \( V_0 \)-graph slope, and fits neither graph.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Graphs of stopping potential \( V_0 \) against frequency \( f \) are drawn for two different metals. The two lines are:
options: Of different slopes, but crossing the frequency axis at the same point
Parallel, with the same slope \( h/e \), but crossing the frequency axis at different threshold frequencies
Parallel, crossing the frequency axis at the same threshold frequency
questions.explanation:
\( V_0=\dfrac{h}{e}f-\dfrac{\phi}{e} \).

The slope \( h/e \) is universal, so the lines are parallel. The intercept depends on \( \phi \), which differs between metals, so they cross the \( f \)-axis at different \( f_0 \).
questions.hint: Which part of the equation contains \( \phi \)?
distractor_logic: This swaps the roles: the slope is universal and the intercept is metal-specific.
Only the slope is universal; different \( \phi \) values separate the lines.
Two parallel lines through the same point would coincide; different \( \phi \) prevents this.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: Light of photon energy 3 eV falls on metal A (\( \phi=2 \) eV) and on metal B (\( \phi=4 \) eV). Which statement is correct?
options: Both emit; A with 1 eV and B with 1 eV
Only B emits, with maximum kinetic energy 1 eV
Only A emits photoelectrons, with maximum kinetic energy 1 eV
Both emit; A with 1 eV and B with 7 eV
questions.explanation:
For A: \( 3>2 \), so \( KE_{max}=3-2=1 \) eV.

For B: \( 3<4 \), so no photoelectric emission occurs from B.
questions.hint: Check each metal against the photon energy separately.
distractor_logic: Taking the size of the difference for B hides the fact that \( hf<\phi \) there.
B needs more energy than the photons carry, so it cannot be the one that emits.
Adding for B ignores that the photon cannot overcome B's work function.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Work Function, and Threshold Frequency
questions.question: For light of frequency \( f \), photoelectrons from a metal have \( KE_{max}=2 \) eV, while \( hf=3 \) eV. If the frequency is doubled to \( 2f \), the new maximum kinetic energy is:
questions.explanation:
\( \phi=hf-KE_{max}=3-2=1 \) eV.

At \( 2f \): \( KE_{max}=6-1=5 \) eV. It more than doubles, because \( \phi \) is fixed.
questions.hint: Find \( \phi \) first; it does not double.
distractor_logic: \( KE_{max} \) is not proportional to \( f \) because of the constant \( \phi \).
Frequency does change the maximum kinetic energy.
This is the new photon energy with \( \phi \) forgotten.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength \( \lambda_{light}=663 \) nm? (Take \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s and \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s.)
questions.explanation:
\( E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{6.63\times10^{-7}} \).

\( E=3\times10^{-19} \) J.
questions.hint: Use \( E=hc/\lambda_{light} \) with the wavelength in metres.
distractor_logic: This is the photon's momentum value, not its energy.
The wavelength was not converted from nm to m.
The number is right but the unit is wrong; the result is in joules.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A photon has energy \( 3\times10^{-19} \) J. Express this in electron volts. (Take \( 1 \) eV \( =1.6\times10^{-19} \) J.)
questions.explanation:
Divide joules by \( 1.6\times10^{-19} \) J per eV.

\( \dfrac{3\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=1.875 \) eV.
questions.hint: To convert J to eV, divide by the electron charge.
distractor_logic: The two numbers were multiplied instead of divided.
The conversion factor was ignored.
A decimal-place slip in the division.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A source emits 3 mW of light of wavelength 663 nm (photon energy \( 3\times10^{-19} \) J). How many photons does it emit per second?
questions.explanation:
Photons per second \( =\dfrac{P}{E} \), with \( P=3\times10^{-3} \) W.

\( n=\dfrac{3\times10^{-3}}{3\times10^{-19}}=1\times10^{16} \) per second.
questions.hint: Power is energy per second; divide by energy per photon.
distractor_logic: The ratio was inverted, \( E/P \).
3 mW was read as 3 W.
Power and photon energy were multiplied.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A photon has energy \( 6.63\times10^{-19} \) J. What is its frequency? (Take \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s.)
questions.hint: Rearrange \( E=hf \).
distractor_logic: The ratio was inverted, \( h/E \).
This is \( E/c \), the photon's momentum, not its frequency.
This is \( c/f \), the wavelength in metres, labelled as a frequency.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A photon has energy \( 3\times10^{-19} \) J. What is its momentum? (Take \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s.)
questions.explanation:
For a photon, \( p=\dfrac{E}{c} \).

\( p=\dfrac{3\times10^{-19}}{3\times10^{8}}=1\times10^{-27} \) kg m/s.
questions.hint: Photon momentum is energy divided by \( c \).
distractor_logic: Energy was multiplied by \( c \) instead of divided.
Energy and momentum are different quantities with different units.
The ratio was inverted, \( c/E \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: A red lamp (700 nm) and a violet lamp (400 nm) each emit the same power. Which emits more photons per second?
options: The violet lamp, since violet photons are more energetic
The red lamp, since each red photon carries less energy
Both emit equal numbers, since the powers are equal
The violet lamp, since its wavelength is shorter so photons are packed closer
questions.explanation:
Photons per second \( =\dfrac{P}{E} \) and \( E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{light}} \).

Red photons have lower energy, so at the same power more of them are emitted per second.
questions.hint: Same power; which photon is 'cheaper' in energy?
distractor_logic: More energetic photons means FEWER of them for the same power.
Equal power does not mean equal photon numbers when photon energies differ.
Wavelength spacing is not how photon number is decided; \( P/E \) is.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: Photon A has wavelength 400 nm and photon B has wavelength 800 nm. The ratio of their momenta \( p_A:p_B \) is:
questions.explanation:
\( p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda_{light}} \), so \( p\propto\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{light}} \).

\( \dfrac{p_A}{p_B}=\dfrac{800}{400}=2 \).
questions.hint: Shorter wavelength means larger momentum.
distractor_logic: This treats momentum as proportional to wavelength.
Photons of different wavelengths have different momenta.
There is no square in \( p=h/\lambda_{light} \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Photon: Energy, Momentum, and the Particle Nature of Light
questions.question: Which phenomenon cannot be explained by the wave theory of light and requires the photon (particle) picture?
questions.explanation:
Interference, diffraction and polarisation are all explained by waves.

The photoelectric effect (threshold frequency, instant emission, intensity-independent \( KE_{max} \)) needs light to arrive as photons of energy \( hf \).
questions.hint: Which of these involves light knocking electrons out of a metal?
distractor_logic: Interference is a classic wave effect.
Diffraction is a classic wave effect.
Polarisation shows light is a transverse wave.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: An electron is accelerated from rest through 100 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (For an electron, use \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}} \) nm, where \( V \) is the accelerating voltage in volts.)
questions.explanation:
\( \sqrt{100}=10 \).

\( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{10}=0.1227 \) nm, comparable to atomic spacings in crystals.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the voltage first.
distractor_logic: Divided by \( V \) instead of \( \sqrt{V} \).
Multiplied by \( \sqrt{V} \) instead of dividing.
The voltage was ignored altogether.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Which has the larger de Broglie wavelength?
options: It depends on the direction of motion
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}} \), so at equal \( KE \), \( \lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \).

The electron is much lighter, so its wavelength is larger.
questions.hint: At fixed kinetic energy, how does \( \lambda \) depend on mass?
distractor_logic: The heavier particle has the SMALLER wavelength at equal kinetic energy.
Equal wavelengths need equal momenta, not equal kinetic energies.
Direction has no role in the size of \( \lambda \).

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: The accelerating voltage for an electron is increased from \( V \) to \( 4V \). Its de Broglie wavelength becomes:
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}} \).

\( \sqrt{4}=2 \), so \( \lambda \) is halved.
questions.hint: Remember the square root.
distractor_logic: This ignores the square root and uses \( \lambda\propto1/V \).
A larger voltage speeds the electron up and shortens \( \lambda \).
The voltage directly sets the momentum, so \( \lambda \) must change.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: A neutron has momentum \( 3.315\times10^{-24} \) kg m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (Take \( h=6.63\times10^{-34} \) J s.)
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{3.315\times10^{-24}} \).

\( \lambda=2\times10^{-10} \) m, i.e. 0.2 nm.
questions.hint: Divide \( h \) by the momentum.
distractor_logic: The ratio was inverted, \( p/h \).
\( h \) and \( p \) were multiplied instead of divided.
A power-of-ten slip in the subtraction of exponents.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: Why do we not notice the wave nature of everyday objects such as a moving car?
options: Their de Broglie wavelengths are extremely small compared with any object or opening they meet
The de Broglie relation does not apply to large objects
Large objects move too slowly to have a wavelength
Their wavelengths are so large that the waves spread out and cannot be detected
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv} \) with a very large \( m \) gives an extremely tiny \( \lambda \).

Diffraction effects need openings comparable to \( \lambda \), so nothing observable happens.
questions.hint: Estimate \( h/(mv) \) for a car.
distractor_logic: The relation applies to all matter; only the size of \( \lambda \) makes the effect unobservable.
Slower motion would actually increase \( \lambda \), and cars still have tiny \( \lambda \).
Large mass makes \( \lambda \) small, not large.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: An electron has kinetic energy 25 eV. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (For an electron, use \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{KE}} \) nm, where \( KE \) is in eV.)
questions.hint: The square root of 25 is a whole number.
distractor_logic: Divided by 25 instead of \( \sqrt{25} \).
Multiplied by 5 instead of dividing.
Divided by 2 instead of 5.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: A proton and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which has the greater kinetic energy?
options: Both have the same kinetic energy
Neither; equal wavelengths mean zero kinetic energy for one of them
questions.explanation:
Equal \( \lambda \) means equal momentum \( p \).

\( KE=\dfrac{p^{2}}{2m} \), so the lighter electron has the larger kinetic energy.
questions.hint: Same wavelength means same momentum; now compare \( p^{2}/2m \).
distractor_logic: The heavier proton has less kinetic energy at the same momentum.
Equal momenta give equal kinetic energies only for equal masses.
Both particles are moving, so both have non-zero kinetic energy.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: De Broglie Wavelength and the Wave Nature of Matter
questions.question: A graph of de Broglie wavelength \( \lambda \) against \( \dfrac{1}{p} \) for a particle is:
options: A straight line through the origin with slope \( \dfrac{1}{h} \)
A straight line with slope \( h \) and a non-zero intercept
A straight line through the origin with slope \( h \)
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=h\times\dfrac{1}{p} \) has the form \( y=mx \).

So the graph is a straight line through the origin with slope \( h \).
questions.hint: Compare \( \lambda=h(1/p) \) with \( y=mx \).
distractor_logic: The slope is \( h \), not its reciprocal.
A hyperbola results when \( \lambda \) is plotted against \( p \), not \( 1/p \).
There is no constant term, so the line passes through the origin.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In a repeat of the Davisson-Germer experiment, electrons are accelerated through 144 V. What is their de Broglie wavelength? (For an electron, use \( \lambda=\dfrac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}} \) nm, where \( V \) is the accelerating voltage in volts.)
questions.hint: 144 is a perfect square.
distractor_logic: Divided by 144 instead of \( \sqrt{144} \), then rounded.
Multiplied by 12 instead of dividing.
Divided by 6 instead of 12.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In a Davisson-Germer set-up with a fixed crystal, the accelerating voltage is increased. What happens?
options: The de Broglie wavelength increases, so the maximum moves to a larger angle
The de Broglie wavelength decreases, so the diffraction maximum moves to a smaller diffraction angle
The wavelength is unchanged, only the intensity of the peak increases
The diffraction maximum disappears, since fast electrons cannot diffract
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \) falls as \( V \) rises.

For the same crystal spacing, a shorter wavelength is diffracted through a smaller angle.
questions.hint: First decide what happens to \( \lambda \).
distractor_logic: Higher voltage means more momentum, which shortens \( \lambda \).
The wavelength depends on the voltage, so it must change.
Faster electrons still diffract; only the angle changes.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Why are thermal (slow) neutrons useful for studying crystal structures by diffraction?
options: They carry charge and are strongly deflected by the atoms
They have no de Broglie wavelength, so they travel straight
Their de Broglie wavelength is comparable to the spacing between atoms in crystals
Their wavelength is much larger than a centimetre
questions.explanation:
Slow neutrons have wavelengths of about 0.1 nm, similar to atomic spacings.

So they diffract strongly from crystals, just like X-rays and electrons.
questions.hint: Diffraction needs wavelength close to atomic spacing.
distractor_logic: Neutrons are neutral; their diffraction has nothing to do with charge.
All moving neutrons have de Broglie wavelengths.
A centimetre-scale wavelength would not diffract from atomic planes.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: If protons were used instead of electrons in a Davisson-Germer experiment at the same accelerating voltage, their de Broglie wavelength would be:
options: Much larger, because the proton is much heavier
The same, because the charges have the same magnitude
Zero, because protons do not have matter waves
Much smaller, because the proton is much heavier
questions.explanation:
Same charge magnitude and same \( V \) give the same kinetic energy.

\( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}} \), so the heavier proton has a much smaller wavelength.
questions.hint: At equal kinetic energy, \( \lambda\propto1/\sqrt{m} \).
distractor_logic: A heavier particle has the smaller wavelength at equal kinetic energy.
Equal charge gives equal kinetic energy, but the masses still differ.
All matter, including protons, has a de Broglie wavelength.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, the scattered electron intensity showed a sharp peak at \( 50^{\circ} \) for 54 V electrons. This peak is explained as:
options: Constructive interference of electron waves scattered from regularly spaced atomic planes
Photoelectrons released from the nickel by the incident beam
Electrons being attracted to one side by a magnetic field
Random collisions producing more electrons at that angle
questions.explanation:
Electron waves scattered by successive atomic layers reinforce each other only at specific angles.

This gives a sharp maximum, the signature of diffraction.
questions.hint: A sharp peak at one angle is a hallmark of a wave effect.
distractor_logic: The detected electrons are scattered beam electrons, not photoelectrons.
No magnetic field was used to produce the peak.
Random collisions would give a smooth spread, not a sharp peak.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Why does an electron microscope achieve much higher resolution than an optical microscope?
options: The de Broglie wavelength of the fast electrons is far smaller than the wavelength of visible light
Electrons are larger than photons, so they hit more of the sample
Electron beams are brighter than light beams
questions.explanation:
Resolution is limited by the wavelength used.

Electrons accelerated through high voltages have wavelengths far below 1 nm, while visible light is about 400 to 700 nm.
questions.hint: Smaller wavelength resolves finer detail.
distractor_logic: Electrons are always slower than light.
Particle size is not what limits resolution; wavelength is.
Brightness does not improve the fundamental resolution limit.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: Why must the Davisson-Germer experiment be carried out in an evacuated chamber?
options: So that the nickel crystal can emit photoelectrons
Because electrons diffract only in a vacuum by definition
So that electrons are not scattered or slowed by collisions with air molecules
To stop the electrons' de Broglie wavelength from becoming zero
questions.explanation:
Air molecules would randomly scatter the electrons and change their energy.

A vacuum keeps the beam well defined so the crystal's diffraction can be measured cleanly.
questions.hint: What would happen to a thin electron beam passing through air?
distractor_logic: Photoemission from nickel is not part of the experiment.
The vacuum is a practical requirement, not part of the definition of diffraction.
Air cannot make a moving electron's wavelength zero.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Davisson-Germer Experiment and Matter Waves for Different Particles
questions.question: In the Davisson-Germer experiment, which quantity was measured by the detector as the scattering angle was varied?
questions.explanation:
The movable detector counted scattered electrons at different angles, for several accelerating voltages.

A sharp rise in this intensity at \( 50^{\circ} \) for 54 V revealed diffraction.
questions.hint: The detector collected electrons, not light.
distractor_logic: No light was emitted or measured.
Stopping potential belongs to photoelectric experiments.
Electron mass was not being measured.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: Beam P has frequency above the threshold of a metal but very low intensity. Beam Q has frequency below the threshold but extremely high intensity. Which statement is correct?
options: Only beam P causes photoelectric emission
Only beam Q causes photoelectric emission
Both cause emission, and beam Q gives the larger photocurrent
Both cause emission, and beam Q gives the higher maximum kinetic energy
questions.explanation:
Emission needs each photon to have energy at least \( \phi \), i.e. \( f\ge f_0 \).

Beam P satisfies this, so it ejects electrons, though few. Beam Q's photons are individually too weak, so no emission occurs, whatever its intensity.
questions.hint: Ignore brightness; check each beam's frequency first.
distractor_logic: Intensity cannot make below-threshold light cause emission.
Beam Q produces no electrons at all, so it cannot give a larger current.
Intensity never raises maximum kinetic energy, and here Q causes no emission at all.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the light is halved and at the same time its frequency is increased (still above threshold). What happens to the saturation current and to the stopping potential?
options: Both the saturation current and the stopping potential increase
Saturation current decreases; stopping potential increases
Saturation current decreases; stopping potential is unchanged
Saturation current is unchanged; stopping potential increases
questions.explanation:
Intensity equals (photons per second) times \( hf \). Halving intensity while raising \( f \) means even fewer photons per second, so the saturation current falls.

Higher frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy, so \( V_0 \) rises.
questions.hint: Treat the two changes separately: one controls number, the other controls energy.
distractor_logic: Raising frequency does not raise current, and halving intensity lowers it.
This ignores the frequency increase, which does change \( V_0 \).
Halving the intensity cannot leave the saturation current unchanged.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: For a certain light and metal, the stopping potential is 3 V. The collector is now held at \( -2 \) V relative to the emitter. What happens to the photocurrent?
options: It is zero, because the collector is negative
It equals the saturation current, because the fastest electrons still reach the collector
It is non-zero but smaller than the saturation current, because only electrons with kinetic energy above 2 eV reach the collector
It is larger than the saturation current, because the field speeds up the electrons
questions.explanation:
A \( -2 \) V collector removes 2 eV from each electron on its way.

Electrons with kinetic energy above 2 eV (up to the 3 eV maximum) still arrive, but slower ones are turned back. So the current is reduced but not zero.
questions.hint: Compare 2 V with the 3 V needed to stop everything.
distractor_logic: The current is zero only at or beyond \( -3 \) V, the stopping potential.
Saturation needs ALL electrons to arrive; here the slower ones are turned back.
A negative collector retards electrons; nothing can exceed the saturation current.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: A student claims: 'Doubling the intensity of the incident light doubles both the photocurrent and the stopping potential.' Which evaluation is correct?
options: The stopping potential part is correct, but the photocurrent does not change
Both parts are wrong; neither quantity changes
The photocurrent part is correct, but the stopping potential does not change
questions.explanation:
Doubling intensity doubles the number of photons per second, so the saturation photocurrent doubles.

Each photon still has energy \( hf \), so \( KE_{max} \) and therefore \( V_0 \) are unchanged.
questions.hint: Split the claim: one quantity counts electrons, the other measures their energy.
distractor_logic: Accepting the \( V_0 \) part repeats the central intensity trap.
This reverses which quantity intensity affects.
The photocurrent does change with intensity, so 'neither' is wrong.

questions.chapter_name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.topic: Electron Emission and the Photoelectric Effect: Experimental Observations and Laws
questions.question: The saturation photocurrent in an experiment is \( 3.2\times10^{-6} \) A. How many photoelectrons reach the collector each second? (Take \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C.)
questions.explanation:
Current is charge per second: \( I=ne \).

\( n=\dfrac{I}{e}=\dfrac{3.2\times10^{-6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=2\times10^{13} \) electrons per second.
questions.hint: Divide the current by the charge on one electron.
